name: Thirunallar Dharbaranyeswarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Dharbaranyeswarar, with Goddess Bogamartha Poon Mulaiyaal (Praneswari); Shani Bhagavan
summary: The foremost Navagraha temple for Shani (Saturn) in South India, where Shiva is worshipped as Dharbaranyeswarar. Devotees bathe in the Nala Theertham and pray to be freed from the hardships of Saturn.

sections.history: Set in the darbha-grass forest that gives the place its name Dharbaranya, this stone temple grew under Chola patronage and is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams hymned in the Tevaram. Across the centuries it became the most revered Shani sthalam of the south, drawing pilgrims who seek relief from the planet's influence. While Shiva as Dharbaranyeswarar is the presiding lord, it is the shrine of Shani Bhagavan that has carried the temple's fame far beyond the region, sustained by an unbroken tradition of worship tied to the movements of Saturn.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian idiom of the Chola builders, with a gateway tower rising over the entrance and enclosed prakaram courts around the sanctum. Within, the central shrine of Dharbaranyeswarar holds the Shiva linga, while the Goddess Praneswari is honoured in her own shrine. The shrine of Shani Bhagavan, set apart, is the focus of the crowds who circle it in prayer. Close to the temple lies the Nala Theertham, the sacred tank where pilgrims bathe before entering, its waters bound to the legend that gives the place its meaning.
sections.legends: The temple is inseparable from the story of King Nala. Afflicted through the long seven-and-a-half-year period of Shani, Nala lost his kingdom and wandered in misery, separated from his queen Damayanti. Coming at last to Thirunallar, he bathed in the Nala Theertham and worshipped Dharbaranyeswarar, and there Shani released him from his suffering and his fortunes were restored. From this the temple draws its enduring promise: that those burdened by Saturn may find here the ending of their trials, and so pilgrims retrace the king's path of bath and worship.
sections.festivals: The great festival is Shani Peyarchi, the transit of Saturn from one zodiac sign to the next roughly every two and a half years, when immense crowds gather and worship extends far into the day and night. Saturdays are sacred to Shani and draw steady streams of devotees, and Pradosham is observed with special care. Offerings to Shani include black or blue cloth and lamps of sesame oil, made by those seeking relief from the effects of Saturn, whether the seven-and-a-half-year cycle or its lesser periods.
sections.experience: A visit begins away from the sanctum, at the Nala Theertham, where pilgrims bathe before entering wet-haired to worship. Inside, the pace is set by the queue to the Shani shrine, where lamps of sesame oil are lit and black cloth offered in quiet, earnest prayer. On Saturdays and above all on Shani Peyarchi the temple fills to overflowing and the wait grows long, but the mood is one of hope and release rather than fear. Come early, keep patience with the crowds, and let the ritual bath and the circling of the shrine unfold in their own order.

visit.timings: Generally open about 6:00 am to 1:00 pm and 4:00 to 9:00 pm; hours are greatly extended and crowds very large on Saturdays and on Shani Peyarchi. Verify locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected. Since the ritual bath in the Nala Theertham precedes worship, carry a change of clothes.
visit.photography: Photography inside the sanctum is generally not permitted. Follow the instructions of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Thirunallar is in Karaikal district, Puducherry, about 5 km from Karaikal town, the nearest hub. Rail access is via Karaikal or Nagapattinam; the nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli, roughly 150 km away.
